hints: Focus on the very first clue, Z dissolves completely in water before heating, so think about which types of salts are always soluble.
Remember the solubility rule: all nitrates are soluble, but Group 2 carbonates are insoluble or very sparingly soluble.
Now compare the oxides left after heating, MgO gives a sparingly soluble hydroxide while BaO gives a soluble hydroxide, so check which residue would disappear completely in water.
walkthrough:
**Use solubility to narrow down Z**

Z is a white solid that is soluble in water. All Group 2 nitrates are soluble in water.

Group 2 carbonates are insoluble (or for magnesium, only very sparingly soluble), so they would leave solid undissolved.

**Eliminate the carbonates**

This means $\text{MgCO}_3$ and $\text{BaCO}_3$ cannot be Z, because a sample would not dissolve fully at the start.

We are left with the two nitrates: $\text{Mg(NO}_3)_2$ and $\text{Ba(NO}_3)_2$.

**Heat the nitrates to form oxides**

On strong heating, Group 2 nitrates decompose to the metal oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen:
$$2\text{M(NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MO} + 4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$$
So we get $\text{MgO}$ from one and $\text{BaO}$ from the other.

**Test the solubility of the residue**

Shake the oxide residue with water. Magnesium oxide forms magnesium hydroxide which is sparingly soluble, so solid would remain:
$$\text{MgO} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Mg(OH)}_2 \text{ (sparingly soluble)}$$
Barium oxide forms barium hydroxide which is soluble, so everything dissolves with no solid left:
$$\text{BaO} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Ba(OH)}_2 \text{ (soluble)}$$
Only barium nitrate fits both observations.

options.A: Incorrect. $\text{MgCO}_3$ is sparingly soluble, not freely soluble, so it fails the first test that Z dissolves in water. Its residue $\text{MgO}$ is also insoluble.
options.B: Incorrect. $\text{Mg(NO}_3)_2$ is soluble so it passes the first test, but on heating it gives $\text{MgO}$. $\text{MgO}$ with water gives sparingly soluble $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$, so solid would remain, not a clear solution.
options.C: Incorrect. $\text{BaCO}_3$ is insoluble in water, so it fails the first observation immediately. Heating would also give insoluble $\text{BaCO}_3$ to $\text{BaO}$ to $\text{BaCO}_3$ confusion, but solubility already rules it out.
options.D: Correct. $\text{Ba(NO}_3)_2$ is soluble in water. On heating it decomposes to $\text{BaO}$, and $\text{BaO}$ reacts with water to give soluble $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$, so the residue dissolves completely with no solid remaining.
